## Introduction

- Cancer of a solid organ is an uncommon indication for organ transplantation
- **Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC)** is an important exception to that general rule
- HCC is the **most common tumor** treated with whole-organ transplantation
- Listed as the primary indication in approximately **25% of liver transplantations (LTs)**

## Treatment Options for HCC

Existing treatment options include:

- Hepatic resection
- Local ablation
- Liver transplantation (LT)

> In the last 20 years, LT has become the therapy of choice for early-stage malignancy in the setting of cirrhosis.

## Evidence Limitations

- The literature **lacks randomized controlled trials (RCTs)** regarding the treatment of HCC
- Most centers base their practice guidelines on:
  - Local experience
  - Retrospective data
  - Theoretic decision analyses
  - Availability of treatment options

## Historical Context

- First LT performed in a patient with HCC in the **1960s**
- Recurrence has been a concern ever since
- Before the late 1990s, LT for HCC carried **high recurrence rates**
- 2-year survival was only approximately **30%**

## Poor Early Outcomes

The poor outcomes were the result of the consensus at that time:

- **Smaller tumors** → treated with liver resection
- **More advanced disease** → treated with LT

> Discouraging results plagued LT for HCC, until it was noted that subgroups of patients with smaller tumors who underwent LT achieved better outcomes.

## The Milan Trial (1996)

- A group from **Milan, Italy** conducted a prospective trial
- Published in **1996**
- Patients with **smaller tumors** achieved 4-year survival rates of **75%**
- Equivalent to survival for non-HCC patients who underwent transplantation
- Similar results were seen in the **United States**

## Impact of Milan Criteria

- Changes in patient selection, dictated by the **Milan criteria**, allowed similar results to be reproduced at other centers
- The **United Network of Organ Sharing (UNOS)** adopted these criteria in **1998**
- Gave **priority for transplantation** to HCC patients

## Expansion of Indication

- This priority, coupled with the **rise in hepatitis C virus (HCV)** patients (in whom HCC frequently develops), fueled the rapid expansion of this indication for transplantation
- This chapter discusses LT for HCC, concentrating on:
  - Its unique pathophysiology
  - How it relates to diagnosis
  - How it dictates therapy

## HEPATOCELLULAR CARCINOMA — Overview

- HCC is the **fourth most common cause** of cancer-related death
- Accounts for **80% of liver cancers** worldwide
- Fastest rising cause of cancer death in the **United States**
- Develops in the setting of cirrhosis in **more than 90% of cases**

## HCC Risk in Cirrhosis

| Condition | Annual HCC Risk |
|---|---|
| Cirrhosis (any cause) | 2.0%–6.6% per year |
| Viral hepatitis without cirrhosis | 0.4% |

> The risk of HCC development in patients with cirrhosis from any cause is approximately 2.0% to 6.6% per year versus 0.4% for patients with viral hepatitis without cirrhosis.

## HCC Incidence Trends

- The incidence of HCC was previously **rising for decades**
- Even with widespread use of **direct-acting antivirals (DAAs)**, HCV will not be eliminated in high-income countries for another **30 years**
- A large number of patients have lived with HCV cirrhosis for **20 to 30 years** and are aging
- They remain **at risk** for developing HCC

## Hopeful Developments

- **HBV vaccination** may decrease HCC incidence
- **DAA success** for HCV may decrease HCC incidence
- However, the **obesity epidemic** and resultant **nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD)** will generate at-risk cirrhotic patients for the foreseeable future

## Overall Survival Variability

- The overall survival (OS) in patients with HCC varies dramatically
- From **2 months** to **greater than 60 months**
- This highlights the importance of an in-depth understanding of this cancer and the options to treat it

## Biology of HCC — Introduction

An understanding of the biology of HCC is critical to assist in clinical decision making about:

- Surveillance
- Treatment

> Although the molecular biology of HCC remains to be fully elucidated, the close association between cirrhosis and the development of HCC is clear.

## Causes of Cirrhosis in the Western World

- **Viral hepatitis** (HBV and HCV)
- **Chronic alcohol use**
- **NAFLD** (nonalcoholic fatty liver disease)

## NAFLD Progression

- NAFLD was an unfamiliar diagnosis as recently as the early 1980s
- Now present in **17% to 30% of Americans**
- Progresses to **NASH** in 32% to 37%
- Then to **cirrhosis** in 5% to 24%

## NAFLD-Driven Cirrhosis

The development of cirrhosis in patients with NAFLD is driven by:

- Repetitive liver injury from **lipid peroxidation**
- **Fatty acid toxicity**
- **Mitochondrial impairment**
- **Oxidative stress**

> 2.6% of patients with NASH cirrhosis develop HCC per year.

## HCC from NASH Cirrhosis — Calculation

A rough conservative calculation:

| Parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| Americans | 330,000,000 |
| × NAFLD prevalence | 17% |
| × Progression to NASH | 32% |
| × Progression to cirrhosis | 5% |
| × HCC development rate | 2.6% |
| **= People developing HCC from NASH/year** | **~23,337** |

## Comparison with HCV

- Prevalence of HCV in the US population: **0.9%** (or 2.3 million people)
- Expected rate of HCC development in this population over 30 years: **about 1% to 3%**

## Viral Hepatitis — HBV Mechanism

- HBV induces **transgene activation**
- **Oncogene transcription**
- **Loss of tumor suppressor genes** as a result of viral DNA integration into the host genome
- HCC will develop in as many as **30% of patients with chronic HBV without cirrhosis**

## Viral Hepatitis — HCV Mechanism

- HCV does **not integrate** into the host genome
- Leads to **chronic inflammation** through continued viral replication
- Rapid hepatocyte turnover in the presence of **oxidative stress** drives the development of multiple **dysplastic nodules**

## Genetic Alterations in HCC

- Unlike some other cancers, **no sequential progression** of genetic defects has been identified
- A **variety of genetic alterations** are usually seen
- Broadly grouped into events that occur either **early or late** in tumor development

## Early and Late Mutations

| Timing | Genetic Alteration |
|---|---|
| **Early** | Inhibition of insulin-like growth factor II receptors |
| **Late** | Loss of heterozygosity of tumor suppressor genes (e.g., **TP53**) |

## Clinically Relevant Aspects of HCC Pathogenesis

The clinician must understand three aspects:

1. The **influence of cirrhosis** on HCC development
2. **Arterial recruitment** of the tumor
3. The tendency for HCC to **invade portal vein (PV) branches**

## Aspect 1: Cirrhosis and HCC Development

- HCC most often develops in the context of **cirrhosis**
- The biology of HCC is related directly to the **environment found in the cirrhotic liver**
- Repeated insult causes **chronic inflammation** driven by:
  - TNF-α
  - TGF-β
  - IL-1
  - From Kupffer cells, endothelial cells, and hepatocytes

## Nodular Regeneration Pathway

- Inflammation stimulates **nodular regeneration** with bridging fibrosis
- Rapid cellular turnover leads to:
  - **Low-grade dysplastic nodules** (mild atypia)
  - **High-grade dysplastic nodules** (at least moderate atypia)
  - **Microscopic foci of HCC**
  - **Frank carcinoma**

## Tumor Cell Contribution

- Tumor cells may secrete **IL-6 and TNF-α**
- Directly contributing to the inflammatory microenvironment
- By activating **Toll-like receptors**

## Field Defect Concept

- Because of the **diffuse nature** of liver injury, multiple tumors can develop at the same time
- If a focus of HCC is removed, **recurrence is most often at a distant site**
- The second tumor is most likely a **second primary tumor**

> The entire cirrhotic organ has the potential for neoplastic conversion — similar to familial adenomatous polyposis in the colon — referred to as a **field defect**.

## FIGURE 108A.1 — Recurrence Pattern

**Recurrence of HCC after ablation** most often occurs at a site **distant from the primary tumor**, suggesting a second tumor was present at the time of treatment that was too small to be detected.

- Recurrence adjacent to primary lesion
- Overall recurrence
- **Recurrence at site different from primary lesion** (most common)

*From Koike Y, et al. Hepatology. 2000;32(6):1216–1223.*

## Aspect 2: Arterial Recruitment

- **Low-grade dysplastic nodules** derive most of their blood supply from the **portal vein**
- **High-grade dysplasia and HCC** are fed by branches of the **hepatic artery** (unpaired with portal tract structures)
- This process is called **arterial recruitment** or **neoangiogenesis**

## Consequences of Arterial Recruitment

- The resulting **hepatic artery dominance** in blood supply produces the characteristically **hyperdense appearance** of HCC
- Used to identify tumors during the **arterial phase of contrast imaging**
- Allows for treatment by **selective hepatic artery embolization**

## Aspect 3: Vascular Invasion

- HCC is known to **invade vascular structures**:
  - **Portal vein** (most typical)
  - Hepatic veins
  - Biliary tree (less frequently)
- The development of vascular invasion is a **key step** in the metastatic potential of the tumor
- Risk of PV invasion is **directly related to size and differentiation status** of the tumor

## Vascular Invasion as Predictor

> Venous invasion is such a strong predictor of metastatic disease that **tumor size and tumor number** can be thought of as **surrogate markers for vascular invasion**.

## Implications for Treatment

- **Microvascular and macrovascular PV invasion** likelihood has implications for treatment decisions
- Evidence of venous invasion on imaging or biopsy **rules out transplantation**
- The probability of recurrence is unacceptably high
- This is why **patients with small tumors** are selected for transplantation

## HCC Screening — Rationale

- Patients with HCC presenting as **symptomatic disease** have a **0% to 10% 5-year survival rate**
- A screening program identifying **early disease** can have a major impact on treatment outcomes
- HCC meets the **World Health Organization (WHO) criteria** for performing screening
- An RCT showed that screening for HCC **reduces mortality**

## Effective Screening Program

An effective screening program:

- Evaluates patients **at risk** for disease
- Uses a **highly standardized** and relatively **inexpensive** test
- Has **high sensitivity**
- Is used if the cost of screening a large population is **less than the benefit** of early detection

## Cost-Effectiveness Threshold

- The ability of a screening program to decrease mortality while remaining cost-effective depends on inclusion of patients with an HCC incidence of **at least 1.4% to 1.5%**

## BOX 108A.1 — Populations for HCC Surveillance

**Causes of Cirrhosis Other Than Hepatitis B:**
- Hepatitis C
- Chronic alcohol abuse
- Hemochromatosis
- Primary biliary cirrhosis

**Hepatitis B Carriers:**
- Asian males ≥40 years
- Asian females ≥50 years
- HBV carriers with cirrhosis
- Family history of HCC
- Africans ≥20 years
- Noncirrhotic HBV carriers with ongoing hepatic inflammatory activity

## BOX 108A.1 (continued)

**Other Predisposing Conditions:**
- Nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH)
- α1-Antitrypsin deficiency
- Autoimmune hepatitis

> These patients with increased but unknown HCC risk should be screened, but no defined surveillance recommendations currently exist.

## Screening for NASH and Other Conditions

- Screening for HCC in patients with cirrhosis from **NASH, α1-antitrypsin deficiency, and autoimmune hepatitis** is **not considered mandatory**
- Most centers include these patients in their screening population
- **Consensus on screening** patients with NASH that do not have cirrhosis is **lacking**

## Alpha-Fetoprotein (AFP) as Tumor Marker

- **AFP** is produced by:
  - Normal fetal hepatocytes
  - Tumor cells
- **Not** produced by healthy, mature hepatocytes
- Traditionally used for:
  - Diagnosing HCC
  - Predicting outcome after resection
  - Screening for recurrence postoperatively

## AFP Performance

- Normal range: **10 to 20 ng/mL**
- Screening cutoff: **20 ng/mL**
- Sensitivity: only about **64%** — making it a **poor screening test**
- Normal AFP levels vary widely across **ethnic backgrounds**
- Lower **positive predictive value (PPV)** in patients with acute viral hepatitis or cirrhosis from viral cause

## AFP Diagnostic Role

- In patients with a liver mass, concomitant serum AFP **greater than 200 ng/mL** carries a very high PPV
- Because of unacceptably low sensitivity and specificity, **AASLD recommended** that serum AFP **no longer be used as a screening tool**
- Still plays a **diagnostic role**
- AFP **greater than 400 ng/mL** is considered diagnostic regardless of ethnic background or cause of liver disease

## AFP and Vascular Invasion

- Serum AFP **greater than 1000 ng/mL** is a strong predictor of **vascular invasion**
- 5-year survival after LT:
  - AFP >1000 ng/mL: **~50%**
  - AFP <1000 ng/mL: **~80%**

> AFP greater than 1000 ng/mL is a **contraindication to LT** at most centers

## AFP Rate of Increase

- A rate of AFP increase **greater than 7.5 ng/mL per month** portends **worse outcome**
- Chemoembolization with subsequent reduction in AFP from >1000 to <500 may result in **satisfactory outcomes**

## Emerging Serum Markers

Research is ongoing to identify better serum markers:

- **AFP-L3**
- **Des-γ-carboxy prothrombin (DCP)**
- **Circulating tumor cells**
- **Cell-free DNA**
- **Neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio**

## Ultrasound (US) Screening

- The most widely used **radiologic screening tool**
- **Sensitivity:** 65% to 85%
- **Specificity:** >90% when used as a screening test
- Performance in patients with cirrhosis is **not as well-defined**
- **Operator dependent**
- Remains superior to any widely available serologic screening test

## RCT Evidence for US + AFP

- A large prospective RCT in China suggests surveillance of high-risk individuals with **US and serum AFP testing every 6 months** reduces HCC-related mortality by **close to 40%**
- Screening compliance was only approximately **60%** — may have dampened the reduction in mortality
- Patients were offered only resection, not transplantation

## Combined AFP and US

- Combined AFP and US surveillance **increases sensitivity**
- But raises the **cost**
- Increases rate of **false-positive results**:
  - AFP alone: 5%
  - Combined screening: 7.5%
- Especially if a **nodule is present**

## AASLD Recommendations

> The AASLD recommends screening patients at risk for HCC with **US alone every 6 to 12 months**.

- Evaluation of serum AFP can be added to US in the event of concerns regarding operator influence
- The use of AFP as the **lone surveillance tool** is **discouraged**

## Small Nodule Evaluation

- Early HCC can be **difficult or impossible** to distinguish from cirrhotic nodules by US
- Suspicious nodule **<1 cm**: evaluate for stability by repeat US at **3- to 6-month intervals** for up to **2 years**
- All **1- to 2-cm nodules**: investigate with a **dynamic contrast-enhanced (CE) imaging modality**:
  - CT
  - MRI
  - US (CEUS not yet adopted in the US)

## CT Screening Considerations

- CT scanning is a frequently used radiologic surveillance tool
- **Radiation exposure** from screening every 6 to 12 months is **considerable**
- Use as a screening test has **only been modeled**
- Cross-sectional imaging tests are the **diagnostic tests** used to confirm HCC
- The screening test should be **different from the confirmatory test**

## LI-RADS System

- The **American College of Radiology (ACR)** published the **Liver Imaging Reporting and Data System (LI-RADS)**
- Standardizes categorization of liver lesions in patients with cirrhosis
- Based on:
  - Arterial phase hyperenhancement
  - Lesion diameter
  - Washout during venous phase
  - Presence of a capsule
  - Threshold growth

## MRI for HCC

- MRI has been slowly increasing as a screening tool
- Proved **sensitive** at detecting HCC in patients with cirrhosis
- MRI with gadolinium-based or iron oxide-based contrast as a screening test is **not well studied**

## MRI vs CT Specificity

| Modality | Specificity for HCC in Cirrhosis |
|---|---|
| MRI (meta-analysis) | 95%–98% |
| CT | 86%–90% |

## MRI Features Specific for HCC

- **Moderate signal strength on T2-weighted images** is specific for HCC
  - Dysplastic and regenerating nodules are not hyperintense on T2 (unless infarcted)
- **Delayed venous phase hypointensity** with concomitant delayed enhancement of the rim
- More **abbreviated MRI protocols** without T2 and DWI correctly characterize **93% to 96%** of lesions

## Gadoxetic Acid-Enhanced MRI

- Increases sensitivity of MRI for lesions **<2 cm** to **92% to 95%**
- Specificity of **96% to 98%**
- Small lesions are frequently **isointense on T2**, making characterization difficult
- It remains to be seen whether CE MRI is **cost-effective** as a screening tool

## Diagnostic Criteria for Nodules

- **≥2 cm** nodule, hypervascular with PV washout on a **single** dynamic imaging study → treated as HCC
- **1- to 2-cm** nodule on **two** confirmatory studies → treated as HCC
- If results are **contradictory** → **biopsy** should be obtained
- **>2 cm** with typical appearance on a single study + AFP **>200 ng/mL** → biopsy **not required**

## Biopsy Indications

- Biopsy should be performed on any **1- to 2-cm lesion** in any patient **without cirrhosis** who has risk factors for HCC
- Biopsies should be read by **expert pathologists**
- Patients with **negative biopsy** results should undergo US or CE imaging every **3 to 6 months**
- **Rebiopsy** if characteristics change

## High-Risk Biopsy Findings

Biopsy results suggesting high risk for progression to HCC:

- **Dysplastic nodules** (low and high grade)
- **Small and large cell change** (formerly "small cell dysplasia" and "large cell dysplasia")
- **Dysplastic foci** (atypia outside of a dysplastic nodule)

## TREATMENT OPTIONS — Overview

- HCC is **not responsive** to traditional cytotoxic chemotherapeutic agents
- **Sorafenib** (oral multikinase inhibitor) prolonged median survival (10.7 vs. 7.9 months) and time to radiologic progression (5.9 vs. 2.8 months) vs. placebo
- **Immunotherapy** is evolving rapidly and showing promise in advanced HCC
- Best options for **early-stage disease** to achieve cure:
  - Local ablation/embolization
  - Hepatic resection
  - Liver transplantation

## Treatment Decision Factors

Treatment decisions should be based on three factors:

1. **Extent of local disease**
2. **Underlying liver disease**
3. **Local organ availability**

> Patients with CTP class A liver disease who have early-stage HCC are candidates for treatment with the goal of long-term survival free of HCC.

## Advanced Disease Presentation

- Because of the **advanced biologic activity** of the cancer, **80% to 90% of patients** will present at a later stage
- Too advanced for surgical resection or transplantation
- Patients with advanced disease or poor functional status should be offered:
  - Sorafenib
  - Immunotherapy
  - Locoregional therapies
  - Palliative care

## Resection Considerations

- In the **rare patient without cirrhosis**:
  - No evidence of venous invasion or metastatic disease
  - Tumor burden limited to one lobe
  - **Resection should be considered**
- In **cirrhotic patients**:
  - Resection invariably leaves **scattered dysplastic nodules** behind
  - The tumorigenic cytokine milieu puts the patient at risk for **second primary tumor**

## Recurrence After Resection

Risk of developing recurrence after resection for HCC in patients with cirrhosis:

| Timepoint | Recurrence Rate |
|---|---|
| 1 year | ~35% |
| 3 years | 40%–50% |
| 5 years | As high as 70% |

> The history of a previous HCC is the **greatest risk factor** in the development of a new primary HCC.

## Rationale for Liver Transplantation

- This **high risk of recurrence** has driven LT as a method to:
  - Remove the **entire precancerous liver**
  - Prevent the development of **subsequent lesions**
- Results of LT have **improved dramatically** in the last 25 years
- Current recurrence rate: **11% to 18%**

## Mortality After Liver Resection

- The mortality rate after liver resection for HCC is **1% to 7%**
- The major cause is **decompensated liver failure**
- Given the risks of HCC recurrence and postoperative liver failure after resection, some **controversy exists** regarding the best treatment strategy

## Current LT Benchmark

- The current **5-year benchmark** is **70% survival** in patients with HCC undergoing LT
- The **long waiting time** experienced in some regions must also be considered
- Risk of **tumor progression** while awaiting LT must be balanced against the **risk of recurrence**

## Decision Analysis: Resection vs. Transplant

A decision analysis from 2000 compared:

- **Primary resection + salvage transplantation** for recurrence
- **vs. Primary LT** in patients with small tumors

> Wait times **shorter than 6 months** favored LT; those **longer than 12 months** favored primary liver resection.

## FIGURE 108A.2 — Cost-Effectiveness

**Mean gain in life expectancy (LE)** and marginal cost-effectiveness ratios provided by orthotopic liver transplantation (OLT) compared with partial hepatectomy as a function of different time delays before receiving a transplant.

| Wait Time (months) | Additional Cost per Life Year |
|---|---|
| 1 | $44,454 |
| 3 | $43,560 |
| 5 | $53,682 |
| 7 | $69,106 |
| 9 | $128,650 |

*From Sarasin FP, et al. Hepatology. 1998;28(2):436–442.*

## Locoregional Therapy While Waiting

- Whether locoregional therapy offers disease control while awaiting LT is **not clear**
- **Maddala and colleagues**: 54 patients with HCC, average of 3 TACE sessions before LT at median of 211 days
  - 8 patients dropped off waiting list
  - 2 for non-HCC reasons, 6 from HCC progression
  - All progression events occurred within **4 months of listing**

## Hayashi and Colleagues Study

- **20 patients** (median of 2 treatments, mean time to transplantation of 343 days)
- 7 patients whose tumors were within Milan guidelines dropped off:
  - 2 for causes unrelated to HCC
  - 1 for decompensation
  - 5 for increased intrahepatic disease
- Time to exclusion for HCC was **<6 months** in 4 of 5 patients
- **No patients** experienced HCC after LT at mean follow-up of 2.9 years

## Fast-Track Strategy

- Prioritize patients to receive transplant **as soon as possible** without pre-transplant treatment
- Takes away the ability to **observe tumor biology** in time
- A subset of patients with newly diagnosed HCC will have **very unfavorable tumor biology**
- Even if transplanted shortly after diagnosis, they are likely to experience **rapid recurrence**

## Fast-Track Concerns

- Patients with small tumors within Milan criteria have approximately **10% risk of recurrence**
- This corresponds to the percentage with aggressive histologic characteristics
- **Fast-tracking** likely would **significantly increase recurrence rates**
- Recurrence rates were significantly higher in:
  - Fast-tracked patients
  - Patients who underwent **LDLT** compared with patients who had longer waiting times
- Fast-track prioritization is **not cost-effective**

## Recommended Waiting Time

> Even for LDLT, a waiting time of approximately **6 months** is appropriate.

- Patients with large tumor burden initially outside transplant criteria can be **treated until within criteria**
- These patients must then **wait** before undergoing deceased-donor transplant in the US under UNOS policy

## Low-Risk Subgroup (UCSF)

In 398 consecutive patients with stage T2 HCC listed for LT at UCSF:

- Overall risk of being dropped from waiting list: **9.4% at 6 months** and **19.6% at 12 months**
- A subgroup had a **significantly lower risk** of tumor progression

## Low-Risk Subgroup Definition

Regression analysis defined this lower-risk subgroup as:

- **Solitary tumor** measuring 2 to 3 cm
- **AFP level ≤20 ng/mL** after the first locoregional therapy
- **Complete radiologic response** to the initial locoregional therapy

| Group | 1-year dropout | 2-year dropout |
|---|---|---|
| Low-risk subgroup | 1.3% | 1.6% |
| All other HCC patients | 21.6% | 26.5% |

*(P = .004)*

## RFA Before Transplantation

**Mazzaferro and colleagues:**
- 50 patients underwent a single ablation session
- Waited average of 9.5 months before LT
- No waiting list dropouts
- At median follow-up of 22 months, only **2 patients** had cancer recurrence

**Lu and colleagues:**
- 52 patients underwent RFA (mean sessions 1.46)
- After 12 months, 3 patients dropped out
- 41 patients underwent transplantation
- **None** had HCC recurrence at mean follow-up of 15 months

## RFA vs. Resection for Small Tumors

- For small tumors, RFA may be **equivalent to resection** for long-term disease control
- With a **lower risk** of postoperative liver decompensation
- Further trials with long-term outcome data are **required**

## Waiting Time Studies — Samoylva

- Compared recurrence rates in patients with HCC:
  - Waiting **>120 days** for transplant
  - vs. waiting **<120 days**
- The risk of recurrence was **40% lower** in patients waiting more than 120 days for transplant

## Waiting Time Studies — Halazun

- Described outcomes from 10 years of transplanting **10,728 patients** with HCC given HCC priority points
- Compared long vs. short waiting time: **7.6 months vs. 1.6 months**

| Metric | Long Wait | Short Wait |
|---|---|---|
| Risk of death awaiting transplant | 8.4% | 1.6% |
| 5-year survival after transplant | **75%** | 67% |

*(P < .0001)*

## Halazun — Multivariate Analysis

- Shorter waiting time identified as **predictor of worse survival**
- **Hazard Ratio:** 1.545 (CI: 1.375–1.736; P < .0001)
- A good oncologic response to locoregional therapy while waiting for LT portends **lower recurrence**
- The ability to control the rise of serum AFP (AFP response) also portends lower recurrence
- **AFP slope increase <7.5 ng/mL/month** is favorable

## HCV Treatment with DAAs

- Given the limited side effect profile and success of DAA therapy, many patients with HCV complicated by HCC are undergoing **HCV treatment before LT**
- Treatment of HCV with DAAs does **not appear to increase** the risk of mortality or HCC recurrence after LT
- Based on an international multicenter intent-to-treat analysis

## Summary of Treatment Options

- **Resection and ablation**: viable for patients with small tumors without cirrhosis, and for patients with cirrhosis and preserved liver function (normal bilirubin and wedged hepatic vein pressure gradient <10 mm Hg) in regions with very long waiting times
- **LT**: appropriate for patients with tumors within selection criteria and those with small tumors but poor liver function
- A **subgroup** with solitary tumor 2-3 cm, AFP ≤20 ng/mL after first locoregional therapy, and complete radiologic response is at **very low risk** to drop off the waiting list

## Summary — Waiting Time Importance

> Some waiting time before transplant allows the **biology of the tumor to declare itself**, and rushing patients to transplant likely **worsens long-term survival**.

- These observations resulted in the institution of a **6-month waiting time interval** from the time of diagnosis before access to deceased-donor LT in the United States

## INDICATIONS FOR TRANSPLANTATION

- An **unlimited supply** of organs and money would allow for a liberal policy of transplantation for HCC confined to the liver
- Resources are **limited** → efforts must allocate organs to recipients with a high likelihood of long-term survival
- Recurrence risk is clearly **higher** in patients with more advanced disease
- Size and number of nodules in the explanted liver is **directly correlated** with the risk of HCC recurrence

## Selection Criteria

Patients with HCC are evaluated based on three factors:

1. **Tumor size** in centimeters
2. **Number** of radiologically evident tumors
3. **Evidence of PV invasion** or extrahepatic disease

> These factors are a crude but somewhat effective method for predicting overall tumor biology and subsequent risk of recurrence.

## Preoperative Staging (UNOS)

- **Triple-phase CT scan** of the abdomen to quantify intrahepatic disease burden
- **CT scan of the chest** to look for extrahepatic disease
- Can also be accomplished with **MRI of the abdomen** and **noncontrast CT of the chest**

## Limitations of Imaging

- These imaging modalities — the gold standard for HCC imaging — **understage about 20% of patients**
- Can sometimes also **overestimate** actual tumor burden
- When explant or resection pathologic correlation is used:
  - CT scan: only **37% to 75%** sensitive at detecting HCC in cirrhotic liver
  - MRI with gadoxetic acid-enhanced and DWI: **68% to 97%** sensitive
- **Bone scintigraphy** is no longer used because of low sensitivity and specificity

## TNM Staging System

- In the United States, the **modified TNM staging system** of the **American Liver Tumor Study Group (ALTSG)** is used to allocate livers from deceased-donors to patients with HCC
- The original transplantation criteria from the mid-1990s, the **Milan criteria**, are equivalent to **stage I or II** of this TNM classification system
- Using these criteria:
  - Recurrence: **4% to 16%**
  - 5-year survival: **71% to 75%**

## MELD Scoring System

- Implemented in **February 2002**
- Priority was given to patients with **TMN stage T1 and T2 HCC**
- Prioritization was **revised in 2004** to no longer include T1 tumors
- Only patients with **T2 tumors** receive priority listing
- Reason: ~30% of patients with presumed HCC (single lesion ≤2 cm with arterial enhancement) were found to have **no tumor** in their explant

## Milan Criteria — Too Restrictive?

- It has been suggested that the Milan criteria are **too restrictive**
- Size criteria are somewhat **arbitrary**
- Several centers have **extended their criteria** to include highly selected stage III patients
- A retrospective analysis of 1556 patients at 36 centers:
  - 1112 patients with tumor burden exceeding Milan criteria on post-transplant pathologic review
  - 283 patients with no microvascular invasion, tumor burden up to **7 cm** or **7 nodules**
  - This subset achieved **5-year survival of 71%**

## FIGURE 108A.3 — Milan Criteria

**Milan selection criteria for transplantation:**

- **Single lesion**, not >5 cm
- **Up to 3 lesions**, none >3 cm

> Equivalent to stage T1 and T2, respectively, of the American Liver Study Group modified TNM classification system.

## UCSF Criteria

The **UCSF criteria** represent a modest expansion of the Milan criteria:

- **Single tumor** <6.5 cm
- **Maximum of 3 total tumors** with none larger than 4.5 cm
- **Cumulative tumor size** <8 cm

## TABLE 108A.1 — Modified TNM and UCSF Staging

| Traditional Stage | Tumor Burden | UCSF Stage | Tumor Burden |
|---|---|---|---|
| T1 | One nodule ≤1.9 cm | — | — |
| T2 | One nodule 2–5 cm or two to three nodules all ≤3 cm | — | — |
| T3 | One nodule >5 cm or two to three nodules, at least one >3 cm | IIIa | One nodule 5.1–6.5 cm, two to three nodules all ≤4.5 cm, or total diameter ≤8 cm |
| — | — | IIIb | One nodule >6.5 cm, two to three nodules of which one is ≥4.5 cm, or total diameter >8 cm |
| T4a | Four or more nodules, any size | — | — |
| T4b | T2, T3, or T4a plus gross intrahepatic portal or hepatic vein involvement | — | — |

## UCSF Criteria Validation

- A retrospective review of preoperative imaging and explant pathology
- 467 transplantations during a 20-year period
- **Similar 5-year survival** in patients meeting Milan criteria and UCSF criteria:

| Method | Milan | UCSF |
|---|---|---|
| By explant pathology | 86% | 71% |
| By preoperative imaging | 79% | 64% |

- Survival for patients with tumors **beyond UCSF criteria**: **<50% at 5 years**

## Tumor Burden as Surrogate

> Tumor burden is only a **surrogate** for vascular invasion and microscopic metastatic disease, which, along with extrahepatic disease, limits the effectiveness of LT.

## UNOS Downstaging Criteria (2017)

In 2017, UNOS changed the criteria to allow patients with HCC outside the Milan Criteria a pathway to LT, termed **downstaging**.

Eligible for downstaging:

- **Single lesion** between 5 cm and 8 cm
- **Two or three lesions** with one between 3 cm and 5 cm and total tumor diameter <8 cm
- **Four to five lesions** each <3 cm with total tumor diameter <8 cm

> Patients undergo downstaging with locoregional therapy and are eligible for transplant if they have **T2 lesions** after downstaging.

## Impact of Expanded Criteria — Volk Study

- Volk and colleagues examined acceptable outcome risk for transplantation of HCC patients vs. using the organ in a patient without HCC
- On a national basis, expansion of the Milan criteria would **significantly increase waiting list mortality** unless 5-year post-transplant survival for expanded criteria recipients exceeded **61%**
- **Dramatic difference** in the effect of a policy change based on **transplant region**

## Regional Variability

- In regions where the risk of death of non-HCC patients is **low** (low MELD score at LT):
  - HCC criteria could be expanded to allow transplantation with post-transplant survival as low as **25%**
- In regions where there is a **greater need** for transplantation (higher MELD scores) in the non-HCC population:
  - Criteria for transplantation in HCC patients must result in post-transplant survival of **70%**

## 2019 UNOS Allocation Changes

- In 2019, UNOS implemented liver allocation based on **acuity circles**
- Replacing the median MELD at transplant in the DSA or region with the **median MELD at transplant within the acuity circle** surrounding the transplant center
- Patients with HCC are listed with an **initial exception score of 6**
- Six months later, the exception score is increased to the **median MELD at transplant minus 3**, where it remains

## Waiting List Screening for HCC

- Patients awaiting LT are **cirrhotic** and therefore at risk for HCC
- Longer wait times can affect survival
- Average waiting time varies based on:
  - **ABO blood group**
  - **Progression of liver failure**
  - **Geographic location**
- Mean waiting time in the US varied widely (**<6 months to >18 months**) before the 2019 UNOS allocation changes
- For prolonged waiting times, screen patients with **CT or MRI every 3 to 6 months**

## Pre-Transplant Management

- **RCTs** to evaluate different treatment options for patients awaiting LT have **not been completed**
- The sole published series followed patients undergoing **surveillance without local therapy**
  - Showed a **high rate of dropouts** from the waiting list due to tumor progression or liver failure
- Retrospective data suggest cancer-directed therapy should be used if the expected waiting time **exceeds 6 months**

## Pre-Transplant Locoregional Options

Options for pre-transplant locoregional control include:

- **TACE** (transarterial chemoembolization)
- **TARE** with Y-90 (transarterial radioembolization)
- **Ablation** with microwave or RFA
- **Percutaneous cryotherapy**
- **Ethanol injection**
- Or some **combination** of these modalities

## TACE Evidence

- Used by many centers because it offers locally effective treatment with a **low risk of complications**
- Three studies support that TACE may help **reduce attrition** from the pre-transplant waiting list
- Pre-transplant TACE associated with a dropout rate of only **2% to 14%**
- Possible added benefit of **lower post-transplant recurrence rate** (8%–10%)

## TACE Decision Analysis

- The greatest impact of neo-adjuvant TACE (greatest reduction in dropout rate) was in patients transplanted within **4 to 9 months**
- When waiting time was **<4 months**: attrition was similar in treated and untreated patients (20% vs. 34%; P = .08)
- When waiting times **>9 months**: dropout rates re-equilibrated (33% vs. 46%; P = .06)

## TARE vs. TACE

- **TARE** is becoming a commonly used alternative to conventional TACE
- In a recent meta-analysis, TARE offered:
  - **Better overall survival**
  - **Improved oncologic outcome** compared with TACE
- The patient characteristics suggesting which therapy is optimal before LT are **not well characterized**
- Decision varies based on:
  - Tumor location, number, size
  - Degree of synthetic liver dysfunction and portal hypertension
  - Response to previous treatments
  - Local expertise and expected waiting time

## Percutaneous Ethanol Injection (PEI)

- No studies described PEI as a sole treatment in patients awaiting transplantation
- Safe and reliable component of **multimodal therapy** for tumors **<3 cm**
- Uses a small needle, reducing risk of **tract seeding to 0.6%**
- Requires **several sessions** when used as primary treatment
- Prospective evidence supporting it as neoadjuvant therapy is **lacking**

## RFA vs. PEI

- A meta-analysis reported **RFA is superior to PEI** in treatment of small HCC with respect to:
  - Survival and cancer-free survival at 1, 2, and 3 years
  - Tumor response
  - Risk of local recurrence
- Recurrence is more common in patients with tumors **>4 cm**
- In 95%, it occurs within **6 months** and at a site **distant from the primary tumor**

## Radiofrequency Ablation (RFA)

- Induces **tissue necrosis** by delivering heat at the tip of one or several electrodes
- **Major complications:** <10% of patients
- **Mortality:** <1%
- At least as efficacious as PEI for tumors **<2 cm** but requires fewer treatments
- RCTs suggest RFA **improves survival**
- RFA was the preoperative treatment of choice for tumors **>2 cm**
- More recently, **TARE** is also used in these patients

## Downstaging — Rationale

Two observations fueled the current debate:

1. **Not all tumors of the same size** carry the same risk of recurrence
2. It is well documented that **some patients outside the Milan criteria** will benefit from LT

> This has led to efforts to select patients with more advanced disease, but with **favorable tumor biology**, who might benefit from LT.

## Downstaging — Concept

The process of downstaging disease to within Milan criteria may be a mechanism for:

- **Identifying patients** with favorable tumor biology
- **Excluding patients** who do not respond to locoregional ablative therapy
- Allowing time for **unfavorable biology to manifest**

## Downstaging — UCSF Study

- A prospective intention-to-treat analysis evaluated **61 highly selected patients** with tumor stage exceeding T2
- An interval of at least **3 months** was required between treatment and transplantation
- **Downstaging was successful in 70%** of patients
- Remaining patients dropped out, usually from disease progression

## Downstaging — Results

| Metric | Result |
|---|---|
| 1-year post-transplant survival | 96% |
| 4-year post-transplant survival | 92% |

> Carefully selected patients with disease exceeding the Milan criteria can be downstaged with **excellent post-transplant outcome**.

## Downstaging — Updated Results

An update compared 118 patients undergoing downstaging with 488 patients listed for LT with T2 tumors:

| Metric | Downstaging Group | T2 Group | P-value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Received LT after downstaging | 54% | — | — |
| 5-year recurrence-free survival | 90.8% | 88% | .66 |
| 5-year intention-to-treat survival | 56.1% | 63.3% | .29 |

## Importance of Waiting Time in Downstaging

- Median time between first treatment and transplantation: **8.2 months** (Yao study) and **9.8 months** (update)
- This waiting time allows **tumor biology to manifest**
- Patients with more biologically aggressive tumors **dropped out** during the waiting period
- Allowing **selection of lower-risk patients** for transplantation
- A review reinforced: an aggressive downstaging protocol is a **selector of tumor biology** rather than a modulator of tumor behavior

## BOX 108A.2 — UCSF Downstaging Protocol

**Inclusion Criteria for Downstaging:**

- One tumor >5 cm and ≤8 cm
- Two or three lesions, at least one >3 cm but ≤5 cm, and total tumor diameter ≤8 cm
- Four or five lesions, all ≤3 cm, and total diameter ≤8 cm
- **No evidence of vascular invasion** by imaging

## BOX 108A.2 (continued)

**Criteria Defining Success of Downstaging by Imaging:**

- Tumor size and number meeting **UNOS T2 criteria**, or
- **Complete tumor necrosis** by imaging without suggestion of residual tumor

**Criteria Defining Treatment Failure:**

- Death from any cause before liver transplantation
- Exclusion from liver transplantation
- Recurrence of HCC after liver transplantation

## BOX 108A.2 (continued)

**Additional Guidelines:**

- A minimum follow-up period of **3 months** is required before LT, with concomitant imaging studies meeting "success" criteria
- Approval must be obtained by the **regional UNOS review board** for priority listing
- Patients can undergo **LDLT** if a donor is available and imaging studies meet selection criteria
- Patients with **liver decompensation** after downstaging are not eligible unless criteria are met
- In patients treated with resection as downstaging, **microvascular invasion** in the resection specimen is a **contraindication** to LT

## AFP and Downstaging

- A **rising serum AFP** while on the waiting list suggests aggressive tumor biology
- Especially if there is concomitant radiologic evidence of tumor progression after locoregional therapy
- A multicenter European study found **AFP rising at a slope >15 ng/mL/month** was the **best predictor of recurrence** after transplant for patients both inside and outside the Milan criteria

## Large Multicenter Downstaging Cohort

- **4359 LT recipients** with HCC analyzed
- 789 patients with HCC initially beyond Milan criteria
- 465 were downstaged and underwent LT

| Metric | Downstaged Group | Always Within Milan |
|---|---|---|
| 5-year overall survival | 71.3%–68.2% | Lower |
| 5-year recurrence-free survival | 64.3%–59.5% | Lower |

> Response to therapy over time is the **most valuable prognostic indicator** of tumor biology.

## Systemic Therapy Before LT

- The role of systemic therapy in concert with locoregional therapy before LT may be evolving but is **not thoroughly studied**
- Two RCTs showed that the addition of **sorafenib** did **not reduce** waitlist dropout and possibly increased the rate of **biliary complications** after transplant
- Currently, approximately **1% of patients** receive sorafenib before LT

## Immunotherapy Considerations

- Since 2017, immunotherapy with **checkpoint inhibitors (CPIs)** is quickly changing the landscape of treatment for advanced HCC
- **Atezolizumab + bevacizumab** combination therapy is likely to become standard of care in the near future
- CPIs have **not yet been studied** in patients with early or mid-stage HCC
- CPI exposure in the peritransplant period results in **significantly increased risk of graft loss from rejection**
  - As high as **54%** in a small review of patients with liver or kidney transplant

## Technical Aspects of LT in HCC

- LT for HCC presents **technical challenges** requiring special consideration
- Most important: perform the operation based on well-established **oncologic principles**
  - Clear surgical margins
  - Avoiding tumor seeding during the procedure
- The tumor should be handled as little as possible — the **"no-touch technique"**
- Until the **lympho-vascular pedicle** has been ligated

## Hepatic Artery Ligation

- Hepatic artery ligation at the beginning of the hepatectomy can **theoretically limit tumor dissemination** during dissection
- However, **no available evidence** suggests that such an approach lowers the post-transplant recurrence risk

## Prior Therapy Considerations

- The transplant surgeon should be aware of prior therapy
- During **RFA or biopsy**, the needle tract and the diaphragm may be **seeded with tumor**
- If limited diaphragmatic seeding is identified during native hepatectomy:
  - Reasonable to perform **diaphragmatic resection with primary repair**
  - Primary repair of the diaphragmatic defect is usually sufficient
  - **Tube thoracostomy is not required**
- **Diffuse seeding** should preclude LT

## Immunosuppression and HCC Recurrence

- Doses of **corticosteroids** and **antimetabolites** have **not** been found to be independent predictors of recurrence
- High **calcineurin inhibitor (CNI)** levels after transplant are associated with higher recurrence:

| CNI Level | 5-year Recurrence Rate |
|---|---|
| Tacrolimus trough >10 ng/mL or cyclosporine trough >300 ng/mL (first month) | **27.7%** |
| Lower CNI trough levels | **14.7%** |

## mTOR Inhibitors

- In a systematic review of 3666 patients, **mTOR inhibitors** used in patients with greater tumor burden and more vascular invasion achieved **lower rates of recurrence** than patients receiving CNIs
  - **13.8% vs. 8.0%** (P < .001)
- Follow-up periods for mTOR inhibitor patients were considerably **shorter**

## mTOR Prospective RCT

- A prospective international RCT of **525 LT recipients** with HCC compared:
  - mTOR-free immunosuppression
  - vs. conventional maintenance immunosuppression + mTOR inhibitor
- The addition of an mTOR inhibitor **modestly improved recurrence-free survival** up to 5 years after transplant
  - **64.5% vs. 70.2%**
- The effect on recurrence-free survival was most pronounced in patients with **lowest projected risk** of HCC recurrence rather than those with highest risk
- Early addition of mTOR and minimization of CNI may result in **less long-term renal dysfunction**

## Predicting and Screening for Tumor Recurrence

- The propensity of HCC to recur after surgical therapy has spurred investigations of potential **biomarkers**
- **Formalin-fixed tissue** was used for genome-wide expression profiling of normal tissue surrounding HCC
- A reproducible **expression signature** correlated well with survival
- Specific regions of **loss of heterozygosity** have been identified that could quantify a patient's risk of HCC recurrence

## Bone Marrow Micrometastases

- Efforts have been made to identify markers of **extrahepatic tumor spread**
- One attempt: find evidence of **malignant cells in the bone marrow** of patients with HCC
- This could predict recurrence or survival
- However, this practice is **not routinely performed**

## AFP mRNA as Biomarker

- A multivariate analysis of **136 patients** undergoing hepatectomy for HCC
- **Low AFP mRNA levels** identified by real-time quantitative PCR correlated with patient survival and disease-free survival

| Metric | AFP mRNA Negative | AFP mRNA Positive |
|---|---|---|
| 1-year survival | 97% | 86% |
| 3-year survival | 91% | 56% |
| 1-year disease-free survival | 73% | 55% |
| 3-year disease-free survival | 45% | 26% |

*(P < .0001)*

## Post-Transplant Screening

- Screening **all patients** with imaging and serum AFP after transplant is **not cost effective**
- Evidence-based data guiding post-transplant screening of certain populations is **quickly growing**
- Screening **high-risk patients** (defined by adverse histopathologic characteristics in the explanted liver) is a more promising and potentially cost-effective strategy
- **70% to 75% of recurrence** occurs within the first **2 years** after transplantation

## RETREAT Score

- A prognostic score was developed to identify patients who would benefit from post-transplant screening
- Based on:
  - Presence or absence of **microvascular invasion** on the explant pathology
  - **Serum AFP** at time of LT
  - **Sum** of the largest viable tumor diameter and number of viable tumors on explant
- Later **validated on the UNOS database**

## Recurrence After Transplantation

- Therapeutic options are **somewhat limited**
- In approximately **40%** of patients with recurrence, HCC recurs at **extrahepatic sites**
- Chemotherapy is generally **ineffective**
- **Median survival:** only 8.7 to 21.3 months
- Recurrence within **2 years** portends a much worse outcome

## Treatment of Recurrence

| Treatment | Notes |
|---|---|
| **TACE and TARE** | Commonly used; have prolonged survival somewhat |
| **Resection** | ~10% of patients with recurrence can achieve long-term survival |
| **Sorafenib** | Limited success |
| **Immunotherapy (CPIs)** | May have oncologic efficacy but risks severe rejection and graft loss; generally avoided |

## Salvage Transplantation — Concept

- To better maintain the pool of donor organs, some have argued:
  - **Primary liver resection** should be first-line therapy for patients with preserved liver function and solitary HCCs **<5 cm**
  - **Salvage transplantation** can be offered to patients who experience recurrence that falls within the Milan criteria
- In patients with CTP class A with small solitary HCCs, primary resection achieved **5-year survival of 70%**
- Comparable to reported survival after primary transplantation for similar-size tumors

## Salvage Transplantation — Screening

> Screening after resection with **US every 3 months** would be an important aspect of any treatment strategy using salvage transplantation for treatment of recurrence.

- The hope is that if patients recur, they will do so with **transplantable disease** within the Milan criteria

## Salvage LT — Study 1 (Adam et al.)

- Retrospective analysis of **358 patients** with cirrhosis and HCC
  - Transplantation (n=195)
  - Resection (n=163, of whom 98 were transplant candidates)
  - Salvage transplantation (n=17)

| Metric | LT | Resection + Salvage LT |
|---|---|---|
| Operative mortality | 2% | 28% |
| Recurrence rate | 18% | 54% |
| 5-year post-transplant survival | 61% | 41% |
| Disease-free survival | 58% | 29% |

## Salvage LT — Study 2 (Belghiti et al.)

- **88 patients** meeting Milan criteria underwent LT vs. **18** who underwent resection followed by salvage LT

| Metric | Primary LT | Salvage LT |
|---|---|---|
| Morbidity | 51% | 56% |
| 30-day mortality | 5.7% | 5.6% |
| 3-year survival | 82% | 82% |
| 5-year survival | 59% | 61% |
| Recurrence | 3 | 1 |

## Discordant Results — Possible Reasons

- Differences in **time to salvage transplantation**
- Differences in **patient selection**
- Differences in **operative technique** (27% underwent transthoracic resection in the latter study)
- 7 of 18 patients who underwent "salvage transplantation" in the latter study **did not have recurrence**
  - Transplanted for deterioration of liver function or pathologic findings

## Theoretical vs. Actual Transplantability

- Poon and colleagues describe an optimistic rate of patients with recurrence who would theoretically be transplantable after resection: **79%**
- The percentage of patients who have **actually undergone** salvage transplantation, documented in the literature: **1% to 30%**

## Salvage LT — Risk Factors

- **Lee and colleagues**: 114 patients with HCC recurrence after liver resection
  - **Microscopic PV invasion** at resection = risk factor for HCC recurrence after transplant
  - **Satellite nodule** at resection = risk factor for HCC recurrence after transplant
- An intention-to-treat analysis identified predictors of success with salvage LT:
  - **MELD >10**
  - **Absence of neoadjuvant TACE**
  - **Complication-free recovery** from resection
  - **T1 to T2 disease** at the time of liver resection

## Salvage LT — Current Status

- Reports of recurrence after salvage vary widely: **5% to 54%**
- Efficacy of resection followed by salvage transplantation is limited by:
  - Difficulties attending **screening for recurrence**
  - **Prolonged waiting times**
  - **Shortage of donor organs**
- May be a viable option for **patients with HBV without cirrhosis** who have a single lesion

## Future Perspectives — Overview

- LT for HCC offers long-term survival and recurrence-free survival for patients with cirrhosis
- The **shortage of donor organs** is likely to perpetuate interest in resection and salvage transplantation
- Currently, **no consensus exists** about an optimal method to select patients for transplantation after resection

## Future Strategy 1: Histopathologic Selection

- Use well-established histopathologic findings to select patients at **high risk for recurrence** after resection:
  - **Microvascular invasion**
  - **Multiple nodules** unseen on preoperative imaging
- Identification of these findings in the resection specimen could **initiate listing for LT**
- This strategy may select for patients who are at risk for **early recurrence**
- Concern: patients with vascular invasion in explant are at **increased risk for extrahepatic disease**

## Future Strategy 2: Gene-Expression Profiling

- Takes advantage of recent advances in **gene-expression profiling** of fixed liver tissue
- From the liver parenchyma **away from the tumor**
- Can reliably predict risk of **late (de novo) recurrence** by quantifying the **field defect**
- Could theoretically select the population with a field defect at high risk for late recurrence for transplantation
- While allowing those with **low risk** to have resection and be followed
- Remains **investigational**

## Future Strategy 3: Locoregional Therapy + Monitoring

- Treatment of all patients with HCC with **locoregional therapy and downstaging**
- Monitor for **lack of radiographic HCC progression**
- Combined with **low post-treatment serum AFP** that does not rise more rapidly than **15 ng/mL/month**
- Could be used to select candidates for whom transplantation offers a **low risk of recurrence**
- **Relatively low CNI trough levels** after transplant and use of **mTOR inhibitors** are likely to decrease recurrence

## Areas Requiring RCTs

Even with improvements in overall and cancer-free survival in the last 20 years, many areas of HCC treatment require **RCTs**:

- **Preoperative screening**
- **Postoperative surveillance**
- **Downstaging protocols**
- Nontransplant therapies (re-resection, RFA, TACE, TARE, PEI) need to be evaluated against **salvage transplantation** for patients with recurrence
- The role of **systemic therapeutic options** in patients undergoing LT is yet to be defined

## Key Takeaways

- **HCC** is the most common tumor treated with whole-organ transplantation
- **Milan criteria** revolutionized LT for HCC, achieving 71%–75% 5-year survival
- **UCSF criteria** modestly expanded Milan criteria with validated outcomes
- **Downstaging** allows selected patients beyond Milan criteria to access LT
- **Waiting time** of approximately 6 months allows tumor biology to declare itself
- **AFP** remains important for diagnosis and prognosis, though not recommended for screening alone
- **mTOR inhibitors** may reduce recurrence compared to CNIs
- **Salvage transplantation** remains controversial but may be viable for select patients
